svg.title: Bounded streaming and reserved capacity — okfy security explainer
svg.desc: How the tool keeps every read bounded, and how it manages the capacity those reads use. A stream can deliver more data than expected, so buffering a whole response before checking its size would let an attacker allocate memory first and measure later. Every stream the tool reads therefore passes through one bounded reader, readBoundedStream, which pulls bytes and stops at the byte limit with a timeout instead of accumulating an unbounded buffer; decompression goes through the same reader, so inflated PDF object streams, their included streams and their delimiters all share one limit and an oversized stream is discarded rather than kept in part. Capacity is claimed before the read and given back exactly once: a parallel text read reserves bytes and a file slot, an image read reserves bytes, the read runs under the claimed allowance, and a finally block releases the reservation whether the read succeeds, fails or is cancelled; a caller that cannot fit waits for a waiter to be woken rather than overshooting the budget, which is the charged bytes plus the reserved bytes plus the free remainder. One semaphore bounds how many requests are in flight: four at a time, sixty-four may wait, a request beyond that is refused, a thirty-second deadline aborts one that stalls after a slot is granted, and the slot is held through the bounded body read rather than released when the headers arrive, so a slow server cannot multiply itself into an unbounded number of open bodies. When a limit is breached the read is rejected rather than truncated, a failed load or growth is rolled back so the previous bundle stays usable, and a bundle switch cancels the request and releases its slot and reservation. Reserved capacity is released exactly once, on success, failure or cancel, and at most the configured number of requests are in flight through body reading.
svg.text: Reads that stop at a byte limit, capacity claimed before and released after
Every stream is read through the same reader, under a limit
pulls bytes and stops at maxBytes; a timeout aborts a stall
inflates PDF object streams through the same bounded reader
included streams and delimiters share it, so a bomb cannot add up
an oversized stream is dropped, not kept in part
The bound is on the reader, so a size is never measured after the memory has been taken.
Capacity is claimed before the read and given back exactly once
a text read claims bytes and a file slot; an image read claims bytes
the read runs under the claimed allowance, never more
a finally block returns the reservation — success, failure or cancel
a caller that does not fit waits for a waiter rather than overshooting
Reserved capacity is released exactly once — on success, failure or cancel — so a failed read
never leaks the allowance it did not use.
One semaphore bounds how many requests are in flight
MAX_CONCURRENT_FETCHES bounds how many requests run at once
MAX_PENDING_FETCHES caps the queue; a request beyond it is refused
FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS aborts a request that stalls after a slot is granted
the slot covers the headers and the bounded body read, not just the headers
So a slow server cannot multiply itself into an unbounded number of open bodies.
A breach is rejected and rolled back, never absorbed
the read is rejected, not truncated
the growth is rolled back and the previous bundle stays usable
a bundle switch cancels the request and releases its slot and reservation
An over-limit read is dropped and the load is rolled back, so the bundle you had stays usable.
The ceiling is on the tool's own work, not the server's: a bundle may still ask its origin for
every file a link resolves to, each read bounded on the way in.
